questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the glans penis with inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy reveals spirochetes. Which of the following is the treatment of choice?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (chancre) is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. This is the standard WHO and CDC recommended treatment for primary syphilis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with multiple hypopigmented, anaesthetic patches on the trunk and upper limbs with thickened peripheral nerves. Skin biopsy shows foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) filled with acid-fast bacilli. What is the lepromin test reaction in this patient?
questions.exp: This patient has lepromatous leprosy (LL) characterized by diffuse infiltration, numerous bacilli, and poor cell-mediated immunity. The lepromin test (Mitsuda reaction) is negative in lepromatous leprosy due to absent CMI response.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash on the face, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive (titre 1:640). Which antibody is most specific for this diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-dsDNA (double-stranded DNA) antibodies are the most specific for SLE (specificity ~95%) and also correlate with disease activity and lupus nephritis. Anti-Ro and Anti-La are more specific for Sjogren's syndrome.

questions.q: A 60-year-old diabetic man presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base following a dermatomal pattern on the right thorax. He develops severe burning pain that persists 4 months after the rash clears. What is this complication called?
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is defined as pain persisting >3 months after herpes zoster eruption. It is the most common complication of HZV reactivation, especially in elderly and immunocompromised patients. The pain is neuropathic in character.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales on the elbows, knees, and scalp. Auspitz sign is positive. Histopathology would show which of the following?
questions.exp: Psoriasis histopathology shows parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum), suprapapillary thinning, regular acanthosis, dilated tortuous capillaries in papillary dermis, and absence of granular cell layer. Auspitz sign is seen due to exposure of dilated vessels.

questions.q: A 40-year-old patient with morphea presents with indurated hyperpigmented plaques with a violaceous border ('lilac ring'). What is the primary pathological process?
questions.exp: Morphea (localized scleroderma) is characterized by dermal fibrosis with excess collagen deposition replacing normal dermis and subcutaneous fat. The 'lilac ring' represents active inflammation at the expanding border. There is no systemic involvement unlike systemic sclerosis.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters in the mouth and over the trunk that rupture easily leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. ELISA shows antibodies against desmoglein-3. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by IgG antibodies against desmoglein-3 (and -1 in mucocutaneous type). The primary treatment is systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 1-1.5 mg/kg/day). Rituximab is increasingly used as a steroid-sparing agent but systemic steroids remain first-line in acute disease.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with tense blisters on an urticarial base involving the trunk and limbs. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone. What antigen is targeted?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune blistering disorder in elderly patients. It is caused by autoantibodies against BP180 (BPAG2, type XVII collagen) and BP230 (BPAG1). Linear IgG and C3 at BMZ on DIF is characteristic. Nikolsky sign is negative as blister is subepidermal.

questions.q: A 25-year-old HIV-positive male presents with multiple hyperpigmented macules and plaques with new dark violaceous nodules on the legs. Biopsy shows proliferating spindle cells and vascular channels with red cell extravasation. What is the causative agent?
questions.exp: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) in HIV patients (epidemic/AIDS-related KS) is caused by Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8, KSHV - Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus). It presents as violaceous cutaneous lesions and biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces.

questions.q: A 50-year-old fair-skinned man with history of chronic sun exposure presents with an ulcerated lesion on the lower lip that has rapidly grown over 3 months. Regional lymph nodes are palpable. Biopsy shows nests of atypical squamous cells invading dermis with keratin pearls. What is the prognosis-worsening factor?
opts: Location on lip with lymph node involvement
questions.exp: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) on the lip carries a higher risk of metastasis (~15-20%) compared to sun-exposed skin SCC (<2%). Lymph node involvement indicates regional metastasis (Stage III). Poor prognostic factors include: lip/ear location, size >2cm, depth >4mm, perineural invasion, immunosuppression, and lymph node involvement.

questions.q: A 32-year-old immunocompetent patient presents with fever, widespread erythema, and Nikolsky sign positive over large body surface areas. Biopsy shows cleavage at the granular layer with acantholytic cells and no inflammatory infiltrate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) shows subcorneal/intragranular cleavage due to exfoliative toxins (ET-A and ET-B) from S. aureus phage group II that cleave desmoglein-1. There is no inflammatory infiltrate as blistering is toxin-mediated. In contrast, TEN shows full-thickness necrosis with subepidermal cleavage.

questions.q: A 19-year-old presents with multiple comedones, papules, and pustules on the face, chest, and back. Which of the following mechanisms is NOT involved in the pathogenesis of acne vulgaris?
questions.exp: Acne vulgaris pathogenesis involves four key mechanisms: (1) follicular hyperkeratinization forming microcomedones, (2) excess sebum production (androgen-driven), (3) Cutibacterium acnes (formerly P. acnes) colonization triggering inflammation, and (4) inflammation via TLR-2 activation (Type IV/innate immunity). Type III (immune complex) hypersensitivity is NOT involved.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on long-term chloroquine for SLE develops bull's-eye maculopathy on ophthalmological examination. What monitoring is essential before and during this treatment?
questions.exp: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinal toxicity (bull's-eye maculopathy). Baseline ophthalmological examination is mandatory before starting therapy, followed by annual screening. The risk increases significantly after 5 years of use or cumulative dose >1000 g of hydroxychloroquine.

questions.q: A patient presents with itchy, well-defined plaques with a violaceous flat-topped surface and Wickham striae. The most characteristic histological finding would be:
opts: Saw-tooth acanthosis with band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at DEJ
questions.exp: Lichen planus (LP) histology classically shows: hyperkeratosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, irregular acanthosis with saw-tooth rete ridges, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction (DEJ), and basal cell degeneration with Max Joseph spaces. Civatte bodies (apoptotic keratinocytes) are also characteristic.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with painful, tender, bright-red, sharply marginated perianal erash. Swab culture grows beta-hemolytic Streptococcus group A. What is this condition called?
questions.exp: Perianal streptococcal dermatitis (PSD) is caused by Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) and presents with well-demarcated bright erythema around the anus in children. It causes pain, itching, and sometimes rectal bleeding. Treatment is oral penicillin/amoxicillin for 10-14 days.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman with recurrent genital ulcers, oral ulcers, and uveitis is diagnosed with Behcet's disease. Which of the following is a major pathergy-type test used to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: Intradermal prick test producing pustule at 24-48 hours
Skin prick test with grass pollen
questions.exp: The pathergy test (prick test) in Behcet's disease involves a sterile needle prick to the forearm that produces a papule or pustule at 24-48 hours due to non-specific skin hyperreactivity. It is more commonly positive in patients from Middle East and Far East. A positive test contributes to the International Study Group criteria for Behcet's diagnosis.

questions.q: A 24-year-old man presents with annular plaques with central clearing and advancing scaly border on the trunk. KOH mount shows septate hyphae and arthrospores. The infection is caused by:
questions.exp: Tinea corporis (ringworm) is most commonly caused by Trichophyton rubrum worldwide. T. violaceum and E. floccosum are other causes. KOH mount shows septate hyphae. Candida causes satellite lesions with satellite pustules. Malassezia causes pityriasis versicolor with short hyphae and spores ('spaghetti and meatballs' appearance).

questions.q: A neonate develops bullae and erosions at sites of minor friction with scarring and milia formation. Genetic testing shows mutation in KRT5/KRT14 genes. What type of epidermolysis bullosa is this?
questions.exp: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS) is caused by mutations in KRT5 or KRT14 (keratin 5 and 14 genes). It shows intraepidermal cleavage (above basement membrane). The Dowling-Meara type is severe with grouped herpetiform blisters. Junctional EB involves laminin/integrin genes; Dystrophic EB involves COL7A1 (collagen VII).

questions.q: A 26-year-old female runner presents with diffuse hair thinning 3 months after completing a marathon. No scalp scaling, follicular changes, or inflammation is noted. Hair pull test shows increased telogen hairs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium (TE) occurs 2-4 months after a precipitating event (physical/emotional stress, rapid weight loss, surgery, marathon running, postpartum). It causes diffuse shedding with increased telogen hairs on hair pull test. It is self-limiting. No inflammation or follicular changes are seen. Treatment addresses the precipitating cause.

questions.q: A 55-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes presents with a well-defined yellowish-red plaque with waxy atrophic centre and telangiectasias on the anterior shin bilaterally. Biopsy shows palisaded granulomas in the dermis. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) presents as well-defined yellowish-red plaques with waxy atrophic centres and telangiectasias, typically on the anterior shin. Biopsy shows full-thickness dermal necrobiosis with palisaded granulomas. It is associated with diabetes mellitus (66% of cases, but NL occurs in only 0.3% of diabetics). 30% of NL patients do not have diabetes.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with blackheads and papules on the forehead and nose but not the cheeks. His father also had similar involvement. Which variant of acne is this?
opts: Familial acne with preferential nasal-forehead distribution
questions.exp: This presentation suggests familial comedonal acne with predominant involvement of forehead and nose (T-zone). Pomade acne affects the hairline and forehead from hair products. Chloracne (dioxin/chlorinated compounds) produces comedones on cheeks, behind ears, axillae. The familial distribution and typical T-zone involvement supports familial comedonal acne.

questions.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman develops widespread wheals and bullae in the third trimester, with eosinophilia. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows C3 and IgG along the basement membrane zone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP)
questions.exp: Pemphigoid gestationis (herpes gestationis) is an autoimmune subepidermal bullous disorder of pregnancy caused by IgG autoantibodies against BP180 (type XVII collagen). It presents in second/third trimester with urticarial plaques evolving to tense bullae. DIF shows linear C3 (and IgG) at BMZ. PUPPP does not show DIF positivity and does not form bullae.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, calcinosis, and telangiectasias. Antibody testing shows positive anti-centromere antibodies. What is the subset of systemic sclerosis she has?
questions.exp: This is CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias) — the classic presentation of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc). Anti-centromere antibodies (ACA) are found in 70-80% of lcSSc patients and are highly specific. Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) antibodies are associated with dcSSc.

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient treated with phenytoin for epilepsy develops gingival hyperplasia and hypertrichosis. A new blistering eruption develops after sun exposure. Which mechanism explains the phenytoin-induced blistering?
questions.exp: Phenytoin can cause pseudoporphyria — a porphyria-like bullous eruption on sun-exposed areas without porphyrin abnormalities. Other causes include NSAIDs (naproxen is classic), tetracycline, furosemide, and excessive UV exposure. Drug-induced pemphigus is more commonly caused by D-penicillamine and captopril.

questions.q: An 8-year-old child presents with painful lymphadenopathy and a boggy, fluctuant scalp swelling with broken-off hair stubs. Woods lamp examination shows green-gold fluorescence. What is the diagnosis and causative organism?
opts: Kerion due to Microsporum canis/Trichophyton verrucosum
Tinea capitis due to Trichophyton tonsurans
Folliculitis decalvans due to Staphylococcus aureus
questions.exp: Kerion is a severe inflammatory form of tinea capitis caused by zoophilic dermatophytes (most commonly T. verrucosum from cattle and M. canis from cats/dogs). It presents as a boggy, tender, indurated plaque with pustules and lymphadenopathy. Woods lamp shows green-gold fluorescence (Microsporum species). T. tonsurans does not fluoresce.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of facial swelling involving the lips and periorbital area without urticaria. His ACE inhibitor was started 6 months ago. The mechanism of this reaction is:
opts: Bradykinin accumulation due to ACE inhibition
questions.exp: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema is non-allergic, bradykinin-mediated. ACE normally degrades bradykinin; ACE inhibition leads to bradykinin accumulation causing vasodilation and increased vascular permeability. It can occur months to years after starting the drug. It is more common in Black patients. Treatment is drug cessation; icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist) is used for acute attacks.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with small hypopigmented macules with fine scales on the upper trunk. KOH preparation shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. What is the recommended topical treatment?
opts: Selenium sulfide shampoo or ketoconazole shampoo
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor (PV) is caused by Malassezia furfur showing short hyphae and spores ('spaghetti and meatballs') on KOH. First-line topical treatment includes selenium sulfide 2.5% shampoo or ketoconazole 2% shampoo/cream. Terbinafine cream is less effective against Malassezia as it acts on ergosterol synthesis differently. Systemic itraconazole is used for extensive/recurrent PV.

questions.q: A dermatology resident performs a punch biopsy of a suspicious pigmented lesion. After local anaesthesia with 2% lignocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine, the patient develops palpitations and tremors. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Systemic absorption of epinephrine causing sympathomimetic effects
Anaphylaxis to preservatives in local anaesthetic
questions.exp: Palpitations and tremors after local anaesthetic with epinephrine are classic features of systemic epinephrine absorption. This is especially likely if injected into a highly vascular area or inadvertent intravascular injection. Epinephrine causes tachycardia, anxiety, tremors, and elevated blood pressure. True lignocaine allergy is very rare (most are reactions to methylparaben preservative). Vasovagal syncope presents with bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, and Gottron's papules over the metacarpophalangeal joints. Creatine kinase is markedly elevated. What underlying condition must be excluded?
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis (DM) in adults >40 years is associated with internal malignancy in 15-30% of cases (most within 3 years of DM diagnosis). Common associated malignancies include ovarian, breast, gastric, colon, and lung cancers. A thorough malignancy workup (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, tumour markers, PET scan if needed) is mandatory in all adult-onset DM.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man develops a fixed, well-defined oval erythematous patch on the penis that recurs at the same site every time he takes co-trimoxazole. On healing, it leaves post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. What type of drug reaction is this?
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption (FDE) is characterized by a solitary (or few) well-defined round/oval erythematous to dusky plaques that recur at identical sites upon re-exposure to the causative drug. Genitalia and acral sites are commonly affected. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is the hallmark. Most common causative drugs include co-trimoxazole, NSAIDs, tetracycline, metronidazole, and phenolphthalein.
